question: Do subspace activation interventions discovered by Distributed Alignment Search create spurious causal pathways, or does the proposed 'interpretability illusion' test reject legitimate distributed representations too?

key_findings.claim: The reply constructs intuitive causal directions that Makelov et al.'s orthogonal-residual test labels illusory.
key_findings.evidence: Their toy reanalysis decomposes an intervention direction into data-manifold and orthogonal components and shows that a direction regarded as the intended mediator can still leave a causal residual under the test. The argument is that off-manifold effects are inevitable for finite data and do not alone invalidate a high-level causal abstraction.

key_findings.claim: The authors argue that Makelov et al.'s IOI evidence uses directions with very low counterfactual fidelity.
key_findings.evidence: The original single-direction DAS interventions reportedly reach only 0.0-4.2% interchange intervention accuracy even when fractional logit-difference metrics look larger. The reply treats high IIA—100% in the ideal—as the direct test that neural interventions implement the proposed high-level causal model.

key_findings.claim: A reanalysis localizes IOI name-position information to the layer-8 residual stream and distributed attention outputs rather than an MLP direction.
key_findings.evidence: DAS reaches about 70% IIA in the main residual stream but about 4% at MLP activation; attention output reaches roughly 48% and block output about 69%. Individual heads have near-zero IIA, while groups are needed, supporting a distributed-head account.

key_findings.claim: The exchange identifies real validation weaknesses but does not settle how to distinguish an aligned causal abstraction from a flexible intervention that overfits counterfactual labels.
key_findings.evidence: The reply notes IIA limitations, template and entity generalization concerns, source/base pairing choices, and distributed redundancy. Its own alignments are learned on finite counterfactual datasets and ceiling below 100%, so high IIA is graded evidence rather than formal proof unless every intervention is covered.

method.core_idea: Evaluate learned subspace explanations by whether their interventions reproduce a specified high-level causal model across counterfactual inputs, not by whether orthogonal residuals have any effect.
method.mechanism: Formalize the opponent's illusion criterion, construct a counterexample, audit IOI metrics and dataset design, retrain DAS directions at multiple GPT-2 components, measure IIA across templates, and use leave-one-head-out and cumulative-head analyses to trace distributed information flow.
assumptions: The chosen high-level IOI variables are the right explanatory abstraction.
IIA counterfactual pairs cover interventions relevant to the abstraction.
Learned rotations generalize rather than exploit finite templates or names.
Mean/source activation swaps remain within meaningful model states.
Comparing subspaces across streams preserves the intended variable semantics.

techniques.role: Learns a rotated subspace aligned to a causal variable.
Measures agreement between neural and high-level counterfactual interventions.
Tests whether orthogonal causal effects are sufficient to reject an explanation.
Traces name-position information through MLP, attention, and residual streams.
Tests distributed rather than single-head realization.

evaluations.result: An intuitively intended mediator can be labeled illusory
Original-style directions yield only 0.0-4.2% IIA despite larger logit effects
About 70% residual, 48% attention output, and 4% MLP activation at key locations

evaluations.metric: IIA under leave-one-out and cumulative groups
evaluations.result: Individual heads are insufficient; up to 11 heads approach the stream-level ceiling

limitations: The paper is an adversarial reply centered on one task and method family.
IIA below 100% leaves unmodeled mechanisms and is not a proof of faithful abstraction.
Learned intervention subspaces can overfit names, templates, or counterfactual construction.
Off-manifold activation concerns are criticized but not eliminated by the alternative metric.
The empirical reanalysis shares authors with DAS, increasing the value of independent replication.
failure_modes: A high-capacity rotation encodes labels without matching the native computation.
Source/base swaps create states never reached naturally.
A high-level variable is underspecified, making IIA easy or misleading.
Redundant heads allow many distinct alignments with similar IIA.
Template generalization fails on genuinely new linguistic structures.
Fractional logit and IIA metrics disagree because both omit downstream distributional effects.
reusable_insights: Demand counterfactual behavioral fidelity, not merely large logit changes.
Test learned subspaces on unseen entities, templates, and intervention combinations.
Report both on-manifold coverage and off-manifold sensitivity.
Use negative-control high-level variables to measure alignment-search flexibility.
Treat interpretability debates as competing falsifiable validation protocols.
open_questions: What intervention test is both causal and robust to off-manifold states?
How much IIA can a random or semantically wrong variable achieve after alignment search?
Can abstraction fidelity be certified over a combinatorial intervention set?
How stable are DAS directions across seeds, models, and paraphrases?
Can sparse autoencoders or nonlinear alignments be compared under the same protocol?

competitive_landscape.title: Is This the Subspace You Are Looking for? An Interpretability Illusion for Subspace Activation Patching
competitive_landscape.difference: Makelov et al. show learned subspaces can have causal effects through residual/off-manifold directions and warn against face-value interpretation. The reply disputes their sufficiency criterion and attributes empirical cases to weak IIA and evaluation design.

competitive_landscape.title: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
competitive_landscape.difference: Geiger et al. introduce DAS and causal-abstraction alignment. This reply refines its validation story under a direct critique and supplies an IOI stream/head reanalysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Amnesic Probing: Behavioral Explanation with Amnesic Counterfactuals
competitive_landscape.difference: Amnesic probing removes linearly encoded information and measures behavioral change, facing related off-manifold and completeness questions. DAS swaps learned subspaces to test a specified causal abstraction instead.

competitive_landscape.title: Rigorously Assessing Natural Language Explanations of Neurons
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. emphasize controlled prediction/intervention tests for neuron explanations. The same methodological demand motivates this reply's preference for counterfactual IIA over qualitative subspace labels.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The proposed interpretability-illusion definition rejects legitimate explanations, and properly evaluated DAS reveals distributed IOI variables rather than spurious pathways.
novelty_assessment.evidence: A formal counterexample, metric audit, streamwise replication, and distributed-head interventions support the response.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The paper makes a substantive methodological correction and valuable replication, but it is a debate contribution rather than a definitive validation theorem. IIA improves rigor yet still depends on the high-level model, intervention distribution, and alignment-search capacity.

reviewer_notes: Read all 20 extracted pages, including the formal counterexample, full Makelov metric critique, factual-recall caveats, IOI stream/head experiments, conclusion, and appendices. Four primary arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23. Both sides' scope and conflicts were retained rather than treating the reply as adjudication.
